entities.summary: Pope Benedict XI, born Nicola Boccasini, was the head of the Catholic Church and ruler of the Papal States from 22 October 1303 to his death on 7 July 1304. He played a crucial role in the governance of the Church during a period of significant turmoil and power struggles between the Papacy and the Holy Roman Empire. Benedict XI's papacy was marked by efforts to reform the Church and restore its authority, but his efforts were ultimately thwarted by the rise of the Avignon Papacy and the Great Western Schism. The Pope's legacy is also intertwined with the history of the Knights Templar, who were accused of heresy and persecution during his papacy. Despite his efforts to reform the Church, Benedict XI's papacy was cut short by his death in 1304. He was succeeded by Pope Clement V, who would go on to play a key role in the Avignon Papacy. Benedict XI's papacy has been the subject of much historical debate and analysis, with some scholars viewing him as a key figure in the struggle for papal power during the Middle Ages.
